title: Non-linear graphs: exponentials, tangents and areas

tips.title: Every exponential passes through (0, 1)
tips.body: For $y = k^x$, putting $x = 0$ gives $k^0 = 1$ whatever $k$ is. So every one of these curves crosses the $y$ axis at exactly $1$ — and for $y = a \times k^x$ it crosses at $a$. That single point identifies the curve faster than anything else on the page.

tips.title: An exponential never reaches the axis
tips.body: A decay curve gets closer and closer to the $x$ axis but never touches it: $0.8^x$ is still positive after two hundred steps. The $x$ axis is an **asymptote**. A sketch that lands on the axis and runs along it has stopped being an exponential.

tips.title: Draw the tangent long, and use a big triangle
tips.body: A tangent touches the curve at one point without crossing it. Draw it right across the grid, then take two points on your tangent that are **far apart** and easy to read. A small triangle magnifies every reading error; a large one buries it.

tips.title: Say whether your area is an over- or under-estimate
tips.body: Trapezia join the curve with straight chords. Where the curve bends **upwards**, each chord sits above it, so the estimate is **too big**. Where it bends downwards, the chords sit below and the estimate is **too small**. There is a mark for saying which, and for saying why.

why.matters:
A straight line has one gradient and you can read it anywhere on the graph. A curve has a different gradient at every point, and that changes what the graph is **for**: it stops being a lookup table and becomes a record of how fast something is changing and how much of it has happened in total.

The two tools here are the only ones you have for that before calculus. A **tangent** gets you the rate at one instant; the **area** underneath gets you the total. And the exponential is worth its own name because it is the shape of everything whose growth is proportional to its own size — money, populations, a cooling cup, a fading signal.

examples.title: Why debt runs away, and the rule of 72
examples.body:
A card charging 24% a year does not add 24% of the original each year. It adds 24% of whatever is there now, which is the definition of exponential growth. £2,000 left alone becomes £5863 in five years.

Because the growth is proportional to the size, the **doubling time** does not depend on the amount — £200 and £10,000 take exactly as long to double. That single number is what the shape gives you, and the shortcut for it is the rule of 72: divide 72 by the rate. At 24% that says 3 years and the truth is 3.2.

The rule is worth carrying because it stays close across the whole useful range: 3% gives 24 against 23.4, and 12% gives 6 against 6.1. It is the same fact as a half-life, running upwards.

examples.title: The distance hiding under a speed graph
examples.body:
Plot a car's speed against time and the **area** underneath is the distance travelled — because a thin strip is a speed multiplied by a short time, which is a small distance, and the strips add up.

Take a car whose speed in metres a second is $t^2/2$, so after ten seconds it is doing 50 m/s. Split the ten seconds into 5 strips 2 seconds wide, treat each as a trapezium, and the strips total 170 m. The exact answer is 166.7 m, so the estimate is about 2% high.

It is high rather than low for a reason you can see: the curve bends **upward**, so the straight top of each trapezium lies above it and every strip claims a little too much. A curve bending the other way would give an estimate that was too small. Knowing which way you are wrong is often worth more than the estimate.

visual.alt: A speed-time curve rising steeply over ten seconds with the area beneath it shaded, which is the distance the car has travelled

examples.title: A cup of tea, and a tangent that flattens
examples.body:
Tea cools quickly at first and then seems to give up. The reason is that it loses heat in proportion to how much **hotter than the room** it is, so as the gap closes the cooling slows — and the graph of temperature against time is an exponential approaching room temperature rather than a straight line to it.

Take a cup at 90°C in a 20°C room, and a model where the 70°C excess halves every 20 minutes. After 20 minutes it is 55°C, after 40 it is 37.5°C, after 60 it is 28.8°C.

The first 20 minutes cost it 35°C and the third cost 8.8°C — 4 times less, from the same length of time. That falling rate **is** the gradient of the tangent, and it is why adding cold milk at the start keeps tea warmer for longer than adding it at the end.

visual.alt: A falling exponential curve of how far a cup of tea is above room temperature, dropping seventy degrees of excess to half every twenty minutes and flattening as it goes

steps.title: Exponential graphs
steps.body:
An **exponential** has the variable in the **power**:

$$y = k^x.$$

That is a different thing from $y = x^k$, and it behaves very differently. In $y = x^2$ the power is fixed and the base changes; in $y = 2^x$ the base is fixed and the power changes.

**Every exponential passes through $(0, 1)$**, because $k^0 = 1$ whatever $k$ is. For $y = 2^x$:

| $x$ | $-2$ | $-1$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $y$ | $0.25$ | $0.5$ | $1$ | $2$ | $4$ | $8$ | $16$ |

Each step to the right **multiplies** by $2$, rather than adding a fixed amount. That is what makes the curve get steep so quickly.

**Going left, it never gets to zero.** $2^{-1} = 0.5$, $2^{-2} = 0.25$, and so on — always halving, always positive. The $x$ axis is an **asymptote**: the curve approaches it forever and never touches it.

**Two directions.**

- $k > 1$ gives **growth**: the curve rises from left to right.
- $0 < k < 1$ gives **decay**: the curve falls. $y = 0.8^x$ goes $1, 0.8, 0.64, 0.512, \ldots$

**With a multiplier in front**, $y = a \times k^x$ crosses the $y$ axis at $a$ instead of at $1$. A population of $5$ doubling each year is $y = 5 \times 2^x$: it starts at $5$, and after $3$ years it is $40$.

steps.title: The gradient of a curve, at a point
steps.body:
A straight line has one gradient everywhere. **A curve does not** — it is steeper in some places than in others. So asking for "the gradient" only makes sense if you say **where**.

> The gradient of a curve at a point is the gradient of the **tangent** at that point.

A **tangent** is a straight line that touches the curve at that one point without crossing it. On a graph you draw it by eye, and then find its gradient exactly as you would for any straight line.

**The method.**

1. Put your ruler so it touches the curve at the point and matches its direction there.
2. Draw the tangent **right across the grid**, not as a short stub.
3. Pick two points on the **tangent** that are far apart and easy to read.
4. Gradient $= \dfrac{\text{change in } y}{\text{change in } x}$, read off the **axis scales**.

**Use a big triangle.** If your two points are one square apart, misreading by half a square is a 50% error. Twenty squares apart, the same misreading barely shows.

**And read the axes, not the squares.** If one square across is $2$ seconds and one square up is $5$ metres, a triangle of $3$ across and $4$ up is not a gradient of $\tfrac{4}{3}$.

**Say what it means.** On a distance–time graph the gradient is a **speed**; on a speed–time graph it is an **acceleration**. Give the units.

steps.title: Too big or too small, and why
steps.body:
An estimate is only half an answer. The other half is knowing **which way it is wrong**, and that comes from the shape of the curve, not the arithmetic.

Each trapezium replaces a piece of curve with a straight **chord** between its two ends. So:

- where the curve bends **upwards** (it sags below the chord), the trapezium includes area that is not there, and the estimate is **too big**;
- where the curve bends **downwards** (it bulges above the chord), the trapezium misses some area, and the estimate is **too small**.

For $y = x^2$ from $0$ to $4$, four strips gave $22$. The true area is $21\tfrac{1}{3}$, so the estimate was indeed a little too big — exactly as the upward bend predicts.

**More strips is closer.** Doubling to eight strips of width $0.5$ gives $21.5$, which is nearer the true value. Narrower strips mean shorter chords, and a short chord hugs the curve more tightly. The estimate is still too big, because the bend has not changed direction — just less so.

> Narrower strips improve the estimate. They do not change whether it is an over- or under-estimate.

**Saying it properly.** "This is an over-estimate, because the curve bends upwards so each chord lies above it." Both halves earn marks: the verdict, and the reason.

steps.title: Going deeper: reading a tangent properly, and what an estimate is worth
steps.body:
**The commonest way to lose a gradient mark** is to draw the tangent correctly and then measure it wrongly.

Suppose the tangent to a speed–time curve passes through $(2, 6)$ and $(8, 30)$, with time in seconds and speed in m/s.

$$\text{gradient} = \frac{30 - 6}{8 - 2} = \frac{24}{6} = 4.$$

The units come from the axes: metres per second, per second — that is $4$ m/s². The gradient of a speed–time graph is an **acceleration**, not a speed.

**Count in axis units, not squares.** If one square across is $2$ s and one square up is $5$ m/s, then a triangle spanning $3$ squares across and $4$ up is $6$ s and $20$ m/s, and the gradient is $\tfrac{20}{6} = 3.3$, not $\tfrac{4}{3}$.

**Why a symmetric triangle is safest.** On $y = x^2$ at $x = 3$, taking the chord from $x = 2.5$ to $x = 3.5$ gives

$$\frac{12.25 - 6.25}{1} = 6,$$

which is the exact tangent gradient. Taking the chord from $x = 3$ to $x = 4$ instead gives $7$ — noticeably out. Centring your reading on the point of contact is what makes a hand-drawn estimate reliable.

**And an estimate is an estimate.** Mark schemes accept a range, because two people reading the same graph carefully will not agree to three decimal places. Quoting $4.0000$ m/s² from a hand-drawn tangent claims a precision the method does not have; $4$ m/s², or "about $4$", is the honest answer.

visuals.alt: A tangent line on a speed against time graph with two widely separated points marked on it at 2 comma 6 and 8 comma 30, forming a large triangle for reading the gradient

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- An **exponential** has the variable in the power: $y = k^x$. That is not the same as $y = x^k$.
- Every $y = k^x$ crosses the $y$ axis at **$(0, 1)$**, because $k^0 = 1$.
- $y = a \times k^x$ crosses at **$a$**, the starting value.
- $k > 1$ grows; $0 < k < 1$ decays.
- An exponential **never reaches the $x$ axis**. The axis is an asymptote.
- The **gradient of a curve at a point** is the gradient of the **tangent** there.
- Draw the tangent **long**, use a **large** triangle, and read off the **axis scales**, not the squares.
- Give the gradient its meaning and units: speed on a distance–time graph, acceleration on a speed–time graph.
- **Area under a curve** is estimated with strips: $\dfrac{h}{2}[\text{first} + \text{last} + 2(\text{middle})]$.
- Say what the area **means**: distance under a speed–time graph, volume under a flow-rate graph.
- Curve bending **upwards**: chords sit above it, so the estimate is **too big**. Bending downwards: **too small**.
- **More strips is closer**, but does not change which side the error is on.
- An estimate read off a hand-drawn tangent should not be quoted to several decimal places.

questions.skill: estimating an area under a curve
questions.solution: For part a, the first thing to say is what the area means: under a speed against time graph, the area represents the distance travelled. Now apply the trapezium rule. The readings are two seconds apart, so h is two, and there are five readings giving four strips. The rule is h over two, times the first height plus the last height plus twice all the middle heights. That is two over two, times, bracket, zero plus thirty two, plus two times, bracket, five plus twelve plus twenty one. The middle heights add to thirty eight, so twice that is seventy six. Adding thirty two gives one hundred and eight, and two over two is one, so the estimate is one hundred and eight metres. For part b, this is an over-estimate. The speed readings are rising by five, then seven, then nine, then eleven, so the curve is getting steeper and therefore bends upwards. A curve bending upwards sags below the straight chord that joins the ends of each strip, so every trapezium contains a sliver of area that is not under the curve, and the total comes out too big. For part c, acceleration is the rate at which speed changes, which on this graph is the gradient. Since the graph is a curve rather than a straight line, the gradient differs from point to point, so I would plot the points, draw a smooth curve through them, and then place a ruler so that it touches the curve at t equals four without crossing it. That is the tangent. I would draw it right across the grid, pick two points on the tangent that are far apart and easy to read, and work out the change in speed divided by the change in time, reading both off the axis scales rather than counting squares. That gradient is the acceleration at t equals four, in metres per second squared.

questions.prompt:
A colony of bacteria doubles every hour. There are $5$ bacteria at the start.

(a) Write a formula for the number $N$ after $t$ hours, and use it to find $N$ after $3$ hours.

(b) Sketch the shape of the graph of $N$ against $t$, describing where it crosses the vertical axis and how it behaves for large $t$.

(c) A student says "after $10$ hours there will be $50$ bacteria, because $5 \times 10 = 50$." Explain what is wrong with this, and give the correct figure.
questions.solution: For part a, the starting number is five and the multiplier is two, since the colony doubles each hour. So the formula is N equals five times two to the power t, where t is the number of hours. After three hours, two cubed is eight, so N equals five times eight, which is forty bacteria. For part b, the graph crosses the vertical axis at five, because at t equals zero, two to the power zero is one and five times one is five. That is the starting number, which is what the coefficient in front always represents. From there the curve rises, and it rises increasingly steeply: each hour it does not add a fixed amount but multiplies by two, so the steps get bigger and bigger. It is a smooth curve with no straight sections and no maximum, and it never comes back down. For part c, the student has treated the growth as though it were linear, adding the same amount each hour, and has multiplied the starting number by the number of hours. But doubling is multiplication repeated, not addition repeated, so the number of hours belongs in the power, not as a multiplier. The correct calculation is five times two to the power ten. Two to the power ten is one thousand and twenty four, so N equals five times one thousand and twenty four, which is five thousand one hundred and twenty. That is a hundred times the student's figure, which shows how quickly exponential growth outruns linear growth.

examTechnique.body:
**Recognise the exponential by its $y$ intercept.** $y = k^x$ crosses at $1$; $y = a \times k^x$ crosses at $a$. Then check the direction: $k > 1$ grows, $0 < k < 1$ decays.

**Never draw an exponential touching the $x$ axis.** It approaches the axis and stops short of it forever.

**For a gradient at a point**, draw the tangent, then a large right-angled triangle on it. Read the change in $y$ and the change in $x$ off the axes and divide. Show the triangle — the method mark is for the tangent and the triangle, not the number.

**Give the gradient its units and meaning in context.** On a distance–time graph it is a speed in m/s; on a speed–time graph it is an acceleration in m/s².

**For an area, split it into strips.** Use the strip widths the question gives you, form a trapezium for each, and add. The formula is $\dfrac{h}{2}\big[\text{first} + \text{last} + 2 \times (\text{all the middle ones})\big]$.

**Say what the area means.** Under a speed–time graph it is a distance; under a rate-of-flow graph it is a volume.

**And say whether it is too big or too small.** That comes from the way the curve bends, not from the arithmetic.

**An estimate is expected to be approximate.** Mark schemes allow a range, so a sensible answer read carefully off a graph will be accepted.
examinerErrors: Sketching an exponential through the origin instead of through $(0, 1)$.
Drawing a decay curve that meets and then follows the $x$ axis.
Using a chord between two points on the curve instead of a tangent touching at one.
Drawing the tangent correctly and then reading the triangle off the grid squares rather than the axis scales.
Using a tiny triangle, so a small misreading becomes a large error in the gradient.
Giving a gradient with no units, or calling it a speed on a speed–time graph where it is an acceleration.
Estimating an area and not saying whether it is an over-estimate or an under-estimate.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer identifies an exponential from its y intercept rather than from its general shape, and knows the curve approaches the axis without ever reaching it. For a gradient it draws a long tangent and a deliberately large triangle, reads both changes off the axis scales, and then says what the number means in context with its units. For an area it uses the strips the question specifies, applies the trapezium rule cleanly, states what the area represents, and says whether the estimate is too big or too small, giving the reason as the direction the curve bends. And it treats an estimate as an estimate, rather than quoting it to four decimal places.
